summary:
Guam stands under the United States federal framework as an unincorporated territory, and its own local law adds specific protections and specific conditions for trans visitors.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression is prohibited locally. In August 2015 the Guam Legislature passed Bill 102-33 unanimously, banning discrimination in private employment on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, and separately forbidding discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Legal gender recognition requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a trans person must give the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery, after which the Office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed. A 2018 bill that would have permitted legal gender change on judicial permission with a supporting letter from a licensed professional and no surgery requirement was postponed by the Legislature on 13 December 2018 and failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote, so surgery remains the condition.

On partner recognition, chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015, following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

A January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology." It applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence, and indicates the posture of the federal institutions a visitor will encounter on the island.
tangentialFactors:
Private adult consensual homosexual acts have been legal in Guam since the Criminal Code was reformed in 1978. The earlier 1933 penal code, ordained by the Naval Governor and identical to California's, prohibited sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus whether heterosexual or homosexual, with one to ten years imprisonment. The only reported sodomy case, Pennington v Government in the early 1950s, ended in the defendant's favour on procedural grounds when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held the trial court had been without authority to try Pennington without a jury.

Contemporary reporting describes Guam as regarded as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people, with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment, a visible LGBTQ social scene since the 1990s, and an annual Guam Pride held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. These are general LGBTQ findings rather than transgender-specific ones.
localsOnly:
Local employment discrimination protections on grounds of gender identity or expression, and the separate prohibition on discrimination against government employees, bind Guam employers and the Guam government rather than visitors.

Legal gender recognition on Guam requires surgery: the Office of Vital Statistics amends a birth certificate only on a sworn physician statement confirming sex reassignment surgery, and the Motor Vehicle Division amends a driver's licence on the same kind of sworn statement. The 2018 reform bill failed, so residents seeking amended documents must meet the surgical requirement.

Chamorro people have traditionally accepted homosexuality and transgender people; Chamorro society has been described as sexually tolerant, with homosexuality never viewed as taboo but "taken for granted as part of life."
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory's federal-layer claims (passport and travel-document markers, airport screening procedure, the executive order on gender-affirming care funding) belong to the United States parent record and are not restated here.

Whether Guam's local employment-discrimination protections are enforced by a dedicated agency with trans-specific complaint data is not sourced in this inventory.

The military-service executive order's implementation plan, and how it is applied to the military population on Guam, is not sourced beyond the 30-day directive.
